title: Trump Calls Ukraine’s Renewed Strikes on Russian Oil Sites a “Disgrace” – NBC News
body:
President Donald Trump blasted Ukraine’s renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries on Thursday, calling the strikes a “disgrace” and warning that the assaults could further inflate global gasoline prices—a political flashpoint as Republicans brace for the 2026 midterm elections. The former president’s remarks, delivered during a campaign rally in Ohio, marked the latest public effort to pressure Kyiv to curb its military actions that have reverberated through energy markets worldwide.

Ukraine resumed its campaign against Russian energy infrastructure in early March, deploying long‑range missiles to target oil processing facilities in the southern region of the country. The strikes, which the Ukrainian government says are intended to degrade Russia’s ability to fund its war effort, have been condemned by Moscow as “terrorist” attacks and have prompted a wave of retaliatory rhetoric from Western allies. While the attacks have not halted Russia’s crude exports, they have contributed to a tightening of supply that analysts link to the recent uptick in gasoline prices across Europe and North America.

Trump’s condemnation taps into a broader narrative that blames foreign conflicts for domestic economic woes. Since re‑entering the political arena, the former president has repeatedly tied rising fuel costs to “foreign wars” and “energy sabotage,” positioning himself as a defender of American consumers ahead of the upcoming congressional races. Political strategists note that energy affordability remains a top concern for voters in swing states such as Ohio, Pennsylvania and Michigan, where many households are feeling the pinch of higher pump prices. By framing Ukraine’s actions as a direct threat to American wallets, Trump hopes to galvanize a base that is already skeptical of U.S. involvement in overseas conflicts.

The criticism, however, runs counter to the stance of the current administration, which has continued to back Ukraine with military aid while urging restraint in targeting civilian infrastructure. The State Department has warned that strikes on oil facilities could violate international humanitarian law if they cause excessive civilian harm, and it has called for “proportionate” use of force. Nonetheless, the U.S. Treasury has signaled that any disruption to Russian oil exports could complicate global market stability, a concern echoed by European leaders who are already grappling with energy shortages exacerbated by the war.

Energy experts caution that the link between Ukraine’s missile strikes and consumer gasoline prices is indirect but not insignificant. “The Russian refining sector supplies a sizable share of the European fuel market,” explained Dr. Lena Kovacs, a senior analyst at the International Energy Forum. “When those plants are taken offline, even temporarily, it creates a supply gap that can push prices higher, especially when global inventories are already low due to pandemic‑era demand rebounds.” Yet she added that the primary driver of the recent price surge is the broader geopolitical risk premium, which includes sanctions, production cuts by OPEC+ and lingering pandemic disruptions.

As the midterm campaign season intensifies, the debate over Ukraine’s targeting strategy is likely to become a recurring theme in Republican messaging. Critics argue that Trump’s rhetoric oversimplifies a complex conflict and risks undermining U.S. support for an ally fighting a war of aggression. Supporters, meanwhile, view the condemnation as a necessary reminder that foreign policy decisions have tangible consequences for American families.

Looking ahead, policymakers on both sides of the aisle will need to balance the strategic objective of weakening Russia’s war machine with the practical imperative of maintaining stable energy markets. Whether Ukraine will adjust its targeting criteria in response to domestic political pressure in the United States remains uncertain, but the conversation sparked by Trump’s remarks underscores how the war in Eastern Europe continues to shape political calculations far beyond its borders. The coming weeks will reveal whether the “disgrace” label translates into concrete diplomatic shifts or remains a rally‑room slogan in the run‑up to the 2026 elections.
